Look, I'm not trying to judge how people live their private lives. The gay couple two blocks over? They keep their yard nice, they're polite, their business is their business. Same with my neighbor who's been with his girlfriend for years but never married - that's between them.

But there's a difference between tolerance and enabling things that affect everyone else. The guy with the drinking problem who leaves bottles in the garden and gets loud at night - that's not about tolerance, that's about community standards. We tried talking to him, offered to help him find resources, but at some point the rest of us have a right to peace in our own neighborhood.

The infectious disease thing... I mean, if someone's getting treatment and being responsible, fine. But if they're putting others at risk and not being upfront about it, especially around kids, that's a problem. It's not about discrimination - it's about basic safety.

Here's what I've learned: communication works when people actually want to be part of the community. When they're willing to have conversations about how we all get along. But some people just want to do whatever they want without considering how it affects others.

I'm willing to work with anyone who's willing to work with the rest of us. But being tolerant doesn't mean accepting behavior that breaks down what we're trying to build together. There's a difference between accepting people and accepting actions that hurt the community.

The bottom line is respect goes both ways.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*shifting forward, voice becoming more serious*

This is where it gets real for me. I've been laid off twice in the last five years - once when they brought in a crew that would work for half what we were making, and once when the shop just couldn't compete anymore. When you're watching your own community struggle to find decent work, and then you see jobs going to people who just got here... that's hard to swallow.

Look, I get that people are trying to better their lives. My own grandparents came here for opportunities. But they came at a time when there was work for everyone, when the economy was growing. Now? We've got guys I went to trade school with who are still looking for steady work, families in my neighborhood choosing between rent and groceries.

Fairness to me means people who've been here, who've paid into the system, who've followed the rules - they get first shot at opportunities. That's not racist, that's just logical. If my neighbor who's been here ten years, paying taxes, raising his kids here, is competing with someone who just arrived for the same job, my neighbor should have the advantage.

I'm not saying slam the door shut completely. But maybe we slow things down when unemployment is high. Maybe we prioritize work visas based on what jobs actually need filling that locals can't or won't do. 

The balance I'd want? Take care of the people already here first. Make sure they have opportunities. Then, if there's genuine need for more workers, bring people in with the understanding that they're committed to this place long-term, not just looking to make quick money and leave.

It's about being responsible to the community that already exists.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character12_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*rubbing chin thoughtfully, taking time to consider*

You know, I think most of these perspectives have some truth to them, but people get so dug into their corners they stop seeing the whole picture.

The labor shortage thing - yeah, that's real in some places. I've seen farms and restaurants that genuinely can't find workers. But I've also seen situations where they "can't find workers" because they don't want to pay decent wages. If you paid $20 an hour instead of $10, you'd probably find plenty of Americans willing to do that work. So sometimes it's a real shortage, sometimes it's just cheap labor preference.

Cultural diversity can be good - I like having different food options, different perspectives. But it only works when there's still some common ground, some shared values about how we treat each other and what we expect from community members. When people live completely separate lives, that's not diversity, that's just parallel societies.

The security concerns... look, I'm not going to pretend every person coming in is a saint. We need to know who's here, we need background checks, we need some kind of system. But the terrorism angle gets overblown - most crime in my neighborhood isn't from immigrants, it's from people who've been here their whole lives.

The humanitarian thing pulls at me because my family came here seeking better opportunities too. But there's a difference between helping some people and trying to help everyone at once. We can't save the whole world, and trying to might break what we've got here.

What I need to see is honest numbers - real data on jobs, wages, crime rates, not just political talking points from either side.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leaning forward, speaking with conviction*

Complete openness? That's just not realistic. No country can handle unlimited numbers of people coming in at once - the infrastructure breaks down, communities get overwhelmed, and you end up helping nobody well.

Completely shutting the door? That's not who we are either, and honestly, there are jobs that need filling.

I'd go with a combination - job-based admissions with numerical limits that make sense. Here's how I see it working:

First, you look at what jobs actually need workers that Americans aren't filling, even at decent wages. Not just "jobs Americans won't do," but jobs where there's genuine shortage after you've tried to hire locally and pay fairly. Those get priority for work visas.

Second, you set reasonable numbers based on what communities can actually absorb. Maybe it's different for different regions - a growing area might handle more than a place that's already struggling economically.

Third, you prioritize people who are committed to staying and integrating. Not just coming here to work for a few years and send money home, but people who want to learn English, become citizens, put their kids in local schools, be part of the community long-term.

And you enforce it fairly. No looking the other way for some employers while cracking down on others.

The key is making it predictable and manageable. Communities need time to adjust, to build the infrastructure, to help people integrate. When it happens too fast or without planning, that's when you get the tensions and problems that hurt everyone - including the immigrants themselves.

It's about being welcoming but responsible.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character12_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character12_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*pausing, then speaking more softly, as J now rather than Character12_M*

You know, doing this... it was harder than I expected. Not just emotionally, because I miss him, but because I had to really think through how his experiences shaped his views in ways that were different from mine.

What struck me was how much his perspective came from a place of genuine care for his community, even when I didn't always agree with his conclusions. He wasn't coming from hate - he was coming from this deep sense of responsibility to the people around him, to the place he'd built a life in. His family had to fight for acceptance, so he understood both the immigrant experience and the importance of earning your place in a community.

I think I understood better why he got frustrated with what he saw as people wanting the benefits of being here without the commitment to being part of something bigger. For him, belonging wasn't automatic - it was something you built through showing up, contributing, caring about your neighbors.

It made me realize that some of the immigration debates miss this completely. People talk about economics or culture in abstract terms, but for Character12_M, it was about whether his actual neighborhood, his actual community, could thrive. Whether the guys he worked with could feed their families.

I don't know if I agree with all of his policy ideas, but I understand them better now. And I think... I think he'd want people to remember that behind all the political rhetoric, there are real communities with real people trying to make things work for everyone. That's what mattered to him most.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character12_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
You know, for Character12_M, “fairness” wasn’t some abstract idea—it was real, like something you could touch. It came up a lot when he talked about his dad working two jobs and still getting treated like he didn’t matter. He used to say fairness meant everybody should get a shot—doesn’t matter where you’re from, how much money your family has, or what you look like. But it had to be *real*, not just words on a government pamphlet. Like, if the system’s built so that people like us—the ones scraping by, the ones with accents, the ones living in neighborhoods they call "high-risk"—if we’re always the first to get cut when things get tight, then it ain’t fair. He’d say, “Fair don’t mean equal. Fair means seeing what someone actually needs.”

Belonging? That one hit deep for him. Being Hispanic in a town where folks still side-eye a Spanish accent—even after generations—he felt that sting. He wasn’t foreign-born, his parents weren’t even foreign-born, but somehow, people still made him feel like he had to prove he belonged. He told me once, “I was born here, I speak English, I work hard, I pay taxes—what else you want from me?” Belonging, to him, wasn’t about assimilating completely. It was about being accepted as you are. He remembered when the city redid the park and put up signs only in English, even though half the block speaks Spanish at home. That hurt. It sent a message: *you’re here, but you don’t really count.*

Community, though—that’s where his heart was. He volunteered at the youth center near the train tracks, the one nobody funds right. He said community wasn’t about blood or language or even shared culture—it was about showing up. Like when Mrs. Ruiz’s porch flooded and three families, black, white, Guatemalan, Vietnamese—young kids, old men, single moms—they all came with mops and buckets without being asked. That’s what community looked like to him: messy, loud, imperfect, but *together*. He believed a real community protects its weakest, lifts people up when they fall—not waits for permission or proof of citizenship.

He often said, “We’re all just trying to make it. Some of us just started a few steps behind.” And that shaped everything—how he saw fairness, where he felt he belonged, and what kind of community he wanted to build.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character12_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Man, I love that garden. Even when it’s muddy or the fence is falling apart, it feels… real. I’m out there most weekends, hands in the dirt, growing peppers like my abuela used to. And yeah, it’s *all kinds* of people—people from every corner of the world, and some who’ve never left this zip code their whole lives.

I see Maria from Honduras, tending her cilantro patch like it’s gold. Old Mr. Jenkins, 70-something, white as milk, wearing his veteran’s hat, helping kids plant tomatoes. There’s a young couple—Black, queer, adopted a foster kid last year—always bringing fresh bread to share. And then you got folks like Danny, struggling with addiction, but still shows up to water the beans because “it gives him something to do.”

To me, that’s life. That’s normal. I don’t see “diversity” like some brochure. I see neighbors. Some speak broken English, some none at all—but we figure it out. A smile, hand gestures, sharing food. You learn quick: language ain’t the only way to communicate.

But let’s be real—there are tensions. Like when Mrs. Thompson complained about the drum circle on Sundays, said it was “too loud,” “too chaotic.” But that drum circle? It’s Haitian families celebrating, healing, keeping culture alive. She didn’t see that. To her, it was just noise. That’s where communication breaks down. Not because people are bad, but because fear gets louder than curiosity.

And sure, some folks carry diseases—like when Javier had TB and people freaked out, avoided him like he was poison. But instead of shaming? We should’ve made sure he could get treatment without losing his job. Instead of isolation, support.

Same with alcoholism, mental health, whatever. These aren’t “immigrant problems” or “poor people problems”—they’re human problems. And in a real community, you don’t turn your back. You lean in.

So how do we make everyone feel comfortable? Start by listening. Not waiting your turn to talk—*listening*. Respect doesn’t always mean agreement. It means saying, “I see you. You matter here.” Especially when someone’s different. Especially when they’re struggling.

That garden? It’s not perfect. But it grows. Just like us.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah… I’ve seen it all out there. People quick to judge, quicker to whisper. But let me tell you—judgment don’t fix nothing.

Take Luis, lives in the basement apartment. He’s got HIV, been clean from drugs two years now. Some folks stopped letting their kids play near his door after they found out. Not because he’s dangerous—’cause they *think* he is. That ain’t right. That’s fear talking, not facts. Communication? We need more of it. Like, real talk—not flyers from the health department, but someone standing up at the block meeting saying, “This is what HIV actually means today. This is how you *don’t* get it. And this man? He’s fighting every day just to stay on his feet.” Tolerance starts with knowing people, not rumors.

And yeah, some drink too much. My own cousin did—still does, sometimes. Lost his job, lost his wife. But when he was sober enough to help rebuild the garden beds last spring, nobody thanked him. Just side-eye. How you expect someone to change if you never give them a chance to prove they’re trying?

We treat addiction like a moral failure instead of what it often is—pain, trauma, no support. Same with mental health. The Somali woman who wears the hijab and walks her daughter to school every day? Quiet. Keeps to herself. People say she’s “weird,” “closed off.” But I saw her cry once, late afternoon, when her daughter got bullied for her accent. She didn’t have anyone to call. That’s isolation. That’s what happens when we don’t reach out.

Now, about family stuff—unmarried couples, gay couples, trans folks, whatever—it’s 2024, come on. I grew up Catholic, okay? I heard all the sermons. But watching my best friend, Jake, raise two kids with his husband, doing PTA, coaching Little League—that’s family. Realer than half the married folks I know who scream at each other every night. Love and responsibility matter more than a piece of paper or who sleeps in which bed.

But I get it—some older folks, immigrants or not, they were raised different. They don’t understand. So tolerance has to go both ways. I ain’t saying force beliefs down throats. I’m saying: sit together. Share a meal. Let Mrs. Chen taste your empanadas, and you try her dumplings. Let the gay couple babysit your dog. Let the recovering addict fix your fence. Build trust through *doing*, not just talking.

The times we need more communication? Every time someone says, “They’re not like us.” That’s the red flag. Because “us” keeps getting smaller every time we say that. And soon, there’s nobody left but lonely people guarding empty yards.

I believe in a community where you don’t have to hide. Where you can be struggling, healing, loving differently—and still belong. That’s comfort. That’s home. And if we want that, we gotta choose it—every single day.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Look… I’ll be straight with you—when jobs are tight, it *hurts*. I’ve stood in line at temp agencies where half the guys don’t even speak English, but they’ll work for $2 under minimum wage because they’re scared to say no. And I’ve seen U.S.-born folks—black, white, brown—standing right there beside them, same boots, same calloused hands, wondering why nobody’s hiring.

Fairness? Fairness means *nobody gets thrown under the bus*. It don’t mean slamming the door on migrants because we’re scared. It means asking: *why* are jobs so scarce? Why aren’t wages going up? Why is one person working three gigs just to keep the lights on?

See, what ticks me off isn’t that migrant workers want work. It’s that the system lets employers *play us against each other*. Like, “Oh, you want $15 an hour? Cool, this guy’ll do it for $12 and won’t complain.” That ain’t fair—to him, to me, to anybody. That’s exploitation. And it works *because* we’re divided.

I’m from a working family. My dad drove a delivery truck for 20 years—no benefits, no overtime, back full of knots by age 45. He never blamed immigrants. He blamed the boss who wouldn’t fix the van or give him sick days. He said, “They want us fighting each other so we don’t see who’s really getting rich.”

So if I’m talking balance—local residents vs. migrant workers—I don’t see two sides. I see *one side*: people trying to survive. The real imbalance is between labor and power.

But yeah, when resources are low, tensions rise. People get scared. They say, “They’re taking our jobs.” But let’s look closer. Are they really? Or are they doing jobs *nobody else wants*? Meatpacking plants, farm fields, overnight cleaning crews—the kind of work that breaks your body and pays pennies. A lot of “locals” aren’t lining up for those.

And here’s something people forget: many of these migrant workers *are* locals now. They’ve been here five, ten, fifteen years. Paying rent, buying groceries, sending kids to school. Their kids *are* American. So when we talk about “protecting local jobs,” are we really talking about protecting working people—or just using fear to justify shutting doors?

Fairness to me means:
- No worker, documented or not, should live in fear of being crushed just for speaking up.
- If you’re working in this country, you deserve minimum wage, safety protections, dignity.
- We train and support local workers—not by keeping others out, but by investing in skills, childcare, transit, so people can *reach* the jobs.
- And yeah—immigration status shouldn’t decide whether you bleed the same or hurt the same.

Balance? It’s not about counting heads or drawing lines in the sand. It’s about lifting the floor for *everyone*. Because when the floor’s solid, nobody gets left in the dirt.

I’d rather fight for a living wage for all than stand around arguing who deserves it more. That’s the only fairness that lasts.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character12_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright, let’s break it down—because people talk about immigration like it’s one thing, but it’s *everything*. It’s economics, it’s fear, it’s hope, it’s trauma. And if you’re only seeing one piece, you’re missing the whole picture.

First, the good stuff: yeah, immigrants fill jobs people aren’t doing. I’ve worked construction—I *know* who shows up at 5 a.m. when it’s freezing and the roof ain’t finished. A lot of times, it’s guys from Guatemala, El Salvador, Mexico. Not because they’re “stealing” work—but because the pay’s low, the hours suck, and the safety gear’s optional. Nobody else is signing up. Same in nursing homes, farms, kitchens. If all the undocumented workers vanished tomorrow? Half the food on our tables wouldn’t make it there.

And the cultural side? That’s real too. You ever been to a quinceañera in this neighborhood? Or a West African wedding in the park? That energy, that music, that pride—it *adds* to life. It ain’t replacing anything. It’s expanding it. My mom says American food is burgers and fries. But now we got pupusas, jollof rice, pho—all made by someone’s grandma trying to feed their family. That’s not a threat. That’s flavor. That’s life getting richer.

But then you got the fear talk—crime, terrorism, “they’re changing our country.” Let’s be honest: that stuff gets me mad, but I can’t just yell and walk away. I gotta understand *why* people are scared.

Are crime rates higher in immigrant communities? Nah—studies show the opposite. Undocumented folks avoid police at all costs because they’re afraid of deportation. They don’t want trouble. They’re not out robbing places. But try telling that to Mrs. Peterson at the PTA meeting after she saw some news segment linking immigrants to gangs. Fear spreads faster than facts.

And terrorism? Come on. That’s a whole other level of fear-mongering. One guy does something awful, and suddenly every brown person with an accent is suspect? That’s not security—that’s prejudice hiding behind a badge.

Social tensions? *That* part I get. When a new group moves in, things change fast. Rent goes up. Lines at the clinic get longer. Schools get crowded. People feel left behind—especially working-class folks who’ve been ignored for years. So when they say, “We need to slow this down,” I hear them. But what they’re really saying isn’t always about immigrants—it’s, “Why don’t *we* get help?” Why no childcare? No job training? No repairs on our streets? So when a bus full of asylum seekers shows up and gets shelter while local families sleep in cars? That stings. Not because they shouldn’t be helped—but because *nobody* should have to live like that.

Humanitarian angle? That’s where my heart leans. I’m Hispanic—my ancestors came from somewhere too. Not that long ago. My great-grandmother walked across the desert with kids in her arms. Wasn’t “illegal immigration” to her—it was survival. Same with refugees now—Syrians, Ukrainians, Haitians, Afghans. These people aren’t coming here to collect—they’re running from bombs, gangs, starvation. If that was *my* sister, my nephew—would I want the door slammed?

And yeah, some worry immigrants pull wages down. And… okay, *sometimes* that happens—when employers exploit people who can’t speak up. But again, that’s not the immigrant’s fault. That’s the system letting greed win. The answer isn’t to block people—it’s to enforce labor laws, unionize workplaces, make sure *everyone* gets fair pay.

So which views are reasonable?

- The ones about labor shortages? Reasonable.
- Cultural vitality? Absolutely.
- Humanitarian concerns? Deeply reasonable—morally necessary.
- Fear of being left behind? Yeah, I get that—even if it’s misdirected.

What needs more facts and dialogue?

- The crime link. Needs data. Needs community forums where cops and immigrant leaders talk together.
- The wage suppression thing. Needs honest conversation—not scapegoating. Let’s blame the boss who underpays, not the worker who takes the job.
- Security fears? Need transparency. Show people the stats. Bring in refugee families to tell their stories. Fear shrinks when you see faces.

I keep thinking about that garden again. You don’t pull out a plant because it’s different. You make sure the soil’s deep enough for all of them to grow.

That’s what we need—deeper roots. For everyone.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I won’t pretend I want open borders with zero rules—that’s not realistic when schools are overcrowded, hospitals are stretched, and people here can’t even afford rent. But shutting the door completely? That’s cruel. And it’s not who we say we are.

So if I’m picking a mix of policies—something that feels fair, something that works for folks like me, like my neighbors, like the guy sleeping in his car or the asylum seeker at the bus station—I’d go with this:

**Mainly: admit people based on job demand—but with strong protections.**

Here’s why. I’ve worked jobs nobody else wants. So have half the guys I know. If there’s a real labor shortage—like in farming, elder care, construction—then bring people in *to fill those gaps*. But—and this is big—don’t let employers use them as cheap labor. Tie work visas to wage floors, workplace safety, and the right to organize. No more “I’ll call ICE” if you complain about broken equipment or overtime. That protects immigrants *and* local workers. Because when one of us gets crushed, it drags all of us down.

And while we’re at it? Fix the pipeline for *everyone*. Train locals too. Fund community college programs so people like me—high school plus trade school, no fancy degree—can move up. Help displaced workers retrain instead of just telling them to “work harder.” Fairness means opportunity isn’t just for the new arrivals *or* the born-and-bred—it’s for both.

Now, **set reasonable numerical limits**, yeah—but make them flexible. Like, if this year there’s a spike in refugees fleeing violence—Haiti, Sudan, Afghanistan—let the cap adjust. Humanity shouldn’t have a quota. Use regional processing centers, speed up asylum reviews, stop making people wait years in limbo. And for family reunification? Keep it strong. Splitting parents from kids, siblings from each other—that ain’t American. That’s heartless.

As for **refusing entry to all foreign workers?** Hell no. That’s short-sighted. Who’s gonna pick the food? Staff the nursing homes? We’re aging, our birthrate’s low—someone’s gotta do the work. Pretending we don’t need help doesn’t make us stronger. It makes us delusional.

And **complete openness?** I respect the ideal—“Give me your tired, your poor”—but without planning, it overwhelms communities already struggling. Look what happened when they bused hundreds of asylum seekers to cities with no notice. Good intentions, but no support. Families ended up in gyms. Locals got angry. Immigrants felt humiliated. That ain’t dignity. That ain’t integration.

So balance? You plan. You fund. You integrate.

A fair policy, to me, means:
- Work visas tied to real labor needs and worker rights.
- Pathways to legal status for people already here contributing.
- Smart limits, but room to respond to crises.
- Investment in *both* immigrant services *and* struggling communities—language classes, housing, healthcare, job training—for newcomers *and* long-timers.

Because integration don’t happen by itself. It takes effort. Like the garden—we don’t just throw seeds and walk away. We till, we water, we pull weeds together.

Same with people.

I want a system that’s fair not just on paper, but on the ground. Where someone like me—who’s trying to get ahead, pay bills, take care of family—doesn’t see the immigrant down the block as a threat. Where we both know the game ain’t rigged against us. Where we’re not pitted against each other.

That’s the kind of policy Character12_M would fight for. Not perfect. But *just*. And human.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character12_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character12_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. Yeah, I did.

I thought I knew him well—I *did* know him. But doing this—stepping into his voice, really trying to see through his eyes—not just remember him, but *be* him for a while—it brought something out in me.

I realized… he wasn’t just *reacting* to the world. He was *choosing* how to live in it. Even when things were hard, even when people dismissed him, he kept saying, “We can do better.” Not with anger, not with hate—but with this quiet kind of hope that refused to die. I think I’d forgotten how much courage that takes.

And honestly? It made me face some stuff in myself.

When we first started talking about immigration, I’ll admit—I’ve caught myself thinking, “Are there too many people coming?” Not because I’m heartless, but because I see neighbors losing jobs, struggling to pay bills. I used to worry: *Is there enough to go around?*

But channeling him today, I saw how small that thinking is. He didn’t ask “How little can we give?” He asked, “How wide can we make the circle?” And he answered it with action—with showing up at the garden, helping kids who weren’t his, sharing food with people who looked different or spoke different.

He reminded me that fairness isn’t zero-sum. That belonging isn’t earned by proving you’re “one of us.” It’s given—because you’re human.

And on immigration policy? I still don’t have all the answers. But today, I shifted. I used to lean more on rules, limits, control—like if we just manage it “right,” everything will balance. But Character12_M? He cared about systems, sure, but he cared more about *spirit*. The spirit of welcome. The spirit of standing together.

He made me see: if our policies only protect borders and not dignity—if they ease our fears but crush someone else’s hope—then what kind of country are we really building?

So yeah… I feel closer to him now. Like he’s not just a memory, but still speaking. Still challenging me.

And I’ll tell you this—I’m gonna keep listening. Because the man had fire, but it was a fire meant to warm, not burn. And Lord knows, we need that kind of heat right now.
